ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all proposed directors, officers, shareholders and UBOs against the UN Consolidated List, OFAC SDN and Non-SDN lists, EU Consolidated Financial Sanctions List, and Canadian sanctions administered by Global Affairs Canada under the Special Economic Measures Act (SEMA, s. 4), the United Nations Act, and the Justice for Victims of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act (Magnitsky Act), using the Global Affairs Canada Regime Look-up Tool. PEPs are processed at FATF standard: enhanced due diligence on PEPs, family members and close associates, including corroborated source-of-wealth and source-of-funds verification. The enterprise profile (ISIC 6311, voice streaming with in-app purchase rails via Apple IAP and Google Play Billing) is classified Medium_Risk_Enhanced, requiring annual re-screening, adverse-media monitoring, and alignment of transaction monitoring with app-store payment flows.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun: Canada acceded to the Hague Apostille Convention with effect from 11 January 2024. Documents issued in Quebec or federally are authenticated by the Ministere de la Justice du Quebec or Global Affairs Canada respectively; documents originating from non-Hague states require consular legalization at the Canadian diplomatic mission in the state of origin before acceptance in Quebec.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.name_clearance_statutory_basis: Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises, CQLR c. P-44.1, ss. 15-19 and the Regulation respecting the legal publicity of enterprises; Charter of the French Language, CQLR c. C-11, ss. 63-66.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.name_clearance_registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Quebec (REQ) - Registre des entreprises and the REQ name analysis service at https://www.registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca; mandatory NUANS name search report issued by a REQ-designated search house and also recognized by Corporations Canada at https://www.ic.gc.ca/ina for federal incorporations.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.name_clearance_language_and_transliterat: Charter of the French Language, CQLR c. C-11, ss. 63-66: the registered legal name of a Quebec enterprise must be in French. Where the legal name is in English or another language, a French version must be pre-registered and must appear with equal or greater prominence in contracts, signage, invoices, and the app storefront. Transliteration of non-Latin scripts must follow official French romanization rules; names are examined for distinctiveness, descriptiveness, and misleading similarity against the Quebec Register of enterprises and reserved names.
ubo_and_aml_profiling.name_clearance_extension_and_rejection_a: REQ rejection: within 30 days of the refusal notice, the applicant may file an administrative revision request with the REQ under s. 65 of CQLR c. P-44.1; if the revision is denied, an appeal lies to the Court of Quebec under s. 65.1 within 30 days of the revision decision. In parallel, the applicant may immediately submit a new name reservation on a fresh NUANS report. Extension: the REQ 90-day reservation cannot be administratively extended; a new fee and new NUANS search are required. For a federal CBCA incorporation, the 90-day NUANS reservation may be extended to a maximum of 150 days by written request and fee paid to Corporations Canada before expiry.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Registraire des entreprises du Quebec (REQ) - Registre des entreprises and REQ name analysis service at https://www.registreentreprises.gouv.qc.ca; mandatory NUANS search report via REQ-designated search house; federal alternative portal: Corporations Canada name reservation at https://www.ic.gc.ca/ina.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Charter of the French Language, CQLR c. C-11, ss. 63-66: the registered corporate name must have a French version pre-registered and used with equal or greater prominence; transliteration of non-Latin scripts follows official French romanization; the name must not be misleading, non-distinctive, or confusingly similar to a name already reserved or registered in Quebec.
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: On REQ rejection: administrative revision request under s. 65, CQLR c. P-44.1 within 30 days; appeal to the Court of Quebec under s. 65.1 within 30 days of the revision denial; a fresh name application may be filed at any time on a new NUANS report. Extensions: REQ reservations expire at 90 days without extension; a new fee and NUANS search are mandatory. Federal CBCA reservations (90 days) may be extended by up to 60 additional days by written request and fee to Corporations Canada.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Conditional acceptance. The QBCA, s. 19, and the Act respecting the legal publicity of enterprises require a physical registered office in Quebec at which process may be served; a PO Box or mail-only address is invalid. A virtual-office arrangement is accepted only where the provider maintains a verifiable street address in Quebec, executes a service-of-process agency agreement, and the corporation keeps records at a determinate address. For an ISIC 6311 voice-streaming app classified Medium_Risk_Enhanced, banking partners and Apple/Google merchant onboarding typically require a physical operational address; a pure virtual address is disrecommended without a co-working or commercial-space add-on.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Quantified risk: 8-12% in the first 12 months and 25-35% within 36 months for a virtual-office-only posture; the probability rises to 45-55% if annual input tax credits exceed CAD 500,000, if no personnel or records are found at the registered office during a Revenu Quebec verification, or if FINTRAC/Revenu Quebec flags the volume of in-app cross-border payment flows (Apple IAP / Google Play Billing). Maintaining a real Quebec office with active staff reduces the estimate to under 15%.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) - Business Registration Online (BRO) and My Business Account portal (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency.html); Revenu Québec (RQ) - Mon dossier d'entreprise portal (https://www.revenuquebec.ca). Both authorities administer the federal GST/HST and Quebec QST (TVQ) registration regimes under the federal-provincial GSTRQ single-registration cooperation for establishments in Quebec.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: Step 1: Incorporate under the Canada Business Corporations Act or the Quebec Business Corporations Act and obtain the nine-digit NEQ (Numéro d'entreprise du Québec) from the Registraire des entreprises du Québec. Step 2: Register online through CRA Business Registration Online for the 15-character Business Number (BN); CRA issues the RC program account (corporate income tax) and the RT program account (GST/HST) once the registration obligation or voluntary election is triggered. Step 3: Register with Revenu Québec for the QST (TVQ/TQ) account; Quebec-payroll accounts are administered by Revenu Québec rather than CRA, so no federal RP account is required for a Quebec-only workforce. For foreign non-resident digital suppliers: simplified GST/HST and QST registration is available electronically without Canadian legal presence once taxable supplies to Canadian/Quebec recipients exceed CAD 30,000; the same Business Number and a QST number are issued.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Entity_Level_Taxation. A Canadian or Quebec business corporation is a separate legal and tax taxpayer subject to corporate income tax on worldwide income under Part I of the federal Income Tax Act and the Quebec Taxation Act; there is no pass-through or US-style check-the-box classification for corporations. For indirect tax purposes, the entity is a GST/HST and QST registrant above the small-supplier threshold and a non-small supplier of taxable digital services.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: No check-the-box regime exists in Canadian federal or Quebec tax law. Available elections: (i) voluntary GST/HST registration by a small supplier and voluntary QST registration by a QST small supplier; (ii) election under the Excise Tax Act for supplies between closely related corporations to be deemed made for nil consideration; (iii) GST/HST fiscal-unit election enabling qualifying closely related resident corporations to be treated as a single registrant; (iv) GSTRQ combined GST/QST registration election streamlining filings with CRA and Revenu Québec. Hybrid-mismatch rules based on BEPS Action 2 apply to cross-border arrangements and do not provide any domestic opt-out election.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: Value-added GST/QST system: federal Goods and Services Tax (GST) at 5% plus Quebec Sales Tax (TVQ/QST) at 9.975%, both computed on the same tax-exclusive base; combined headline incidence for Quebec supplies is 14.975%. Harmonized Sales Tax (HST) does not apply in Quebec.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 of worldwide taxable supplies (including zero-rated supplies) in any four consecutive calendar quarters for GST/HST small-supplier status; parallel CAD 30,000 threshold for QST small-supplier status, including the digital-economy simplified registration rule for supplies to Quebec consumers over a 12-month period. Revenues from zero-rated export supplies are excluded from the threshold calculation; in-app subscriptions and virtual items sold through Apple IAP and Google Play Billing to Canadian or Quebec consumers are taxable and count toward the threshold.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No real-time fiscal clearance, mandatory API validation, or digital stamping regime is currently in force in Canada or Quebec. Invoices must contain the prescribed GST/HST and QST registration numbers and particulars required under the Excise Tax Act and the Quebec Sales Tax Act, and supporting books and records must be retained for six years. Electronic invoicing is lawful and acceptable to CRA and Revenu Québec; Quebec has announced a phased roadmap toward mandatory business-to-business e-invoicing, but no binding implementation date applies to this business at the compliance date.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: GST zero-rating (0%) applies under Schedule VI, Part V of the Excise Tax Act to supplies of services and intangible personal property made to a non-resident person who is not registered for GST/HST and where the supply is for consumption wholly outside Canada; QST mirror zero-rating applies under the Quebec Sales Tax Act and is administratively harmonized with the federal rules. Voice-streaming subscriptions and virtual-gift sales qualify for zero-rating only where the corporation retains evidence that the end-user is a non-resident of Canada and the service is consumed outside Canada (e.g., ordinary residence metadata, foreign IP/delivery records, contract terms, and payment origin). Zero-rating is denied where the digital supply is deemed to be made in Canada, where the recipient is a GST/QST registrant for use in Canada, or where an App Store platform acting as merchant of record collects Canadian GST/QST under the platform supply rules.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (B13A export declaration with Unique Identifier or C21 form) - required only if physical promotional merchandise or hardware is shipped; for pure cloud voice-streaming services no Canadian customs exit filing is generated, and the documented export invoice set serves as the equivalent evidentiary record

Bill of Lading / Air Waybill with carrier-signed proof of export - required for physical goods consignments; for digital delivery, substitute Apple App Store Connect and Google Play Console settlement reports and disbursement advices evidencing non-Canadian end-user download metadata and foreign destination

Inward Remittance Certificate - evidenced by bank credit advices, SWIFT MT103/MT950 records, and App Store/Google Play payout statements confirming foreign-currency repatriation to the corporation's Quebec bank account within the compliance treasury window
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: CRA and Revenu Québec may reassess beyond the normal four-year limitation period where a zero-rating claim is supported by misrepresentation attributable to neglect, carelessness, or wilful default. Unsupported export claims are clawed back retroactively at the combined 14.975% rate (5% GST plus 9.975% QST) together with prescribed-rate remittance interest, and may attract the gross-negligence penalty (minimum CAD 500 and generally 25% of the understated net tax). Knowingly making false statements or participating in fraudulent export zero-rating is a criminal offence under section 327 of the Excise Tax Act and parallel Quebec provisions, carrying fines up to 200% of the evaded tax and imprisonment of up to five years upon indictment. Apple IAP and Google Play Billing merchant-of-record settlement records are high-visibility audit data points, and CRA and Revenu Québec cross-match platform payout statements against declared zero-rated export revenue to expose mismatches.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada. Canada has no general foreign-exchange administration or mandatory exchange-control authority for ordinary commercial transactions. Applicable oversight may also involve the Department of Finance Canada, the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada, the Canada Revenue Agency, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, the Autorité des marchés financiers for Quebec-regulated derivatives and financial-market matters, and Global Affairs Canada for sanctions and export controls.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar is generally fully convertible for current-account and capital-account transactions. Canada does not generally impose prior approval, capital controls, repatriation restrictions, or compulsory conversion for foreign investment, shareholder loans, dividends, service fees, royalties, or ordinary trade payments. Profit remittance remains subject to available corporate law authority, solvency requirements, applicable withholding tax, transfer-pricing support, treaty eligibility, thin-capitalization and interest-deductibility rules, beneficial-ownership verification, sanctions screening, and bank anti-money-laundering review. Canadian-resident corporations must maintain adequate books and records and may have cross-border reporting obligations, including specified foreign-property reporting, related-party transaction reporting, and information returns where applicable. Non-resident ownership is generally permitted, but federal or provincial corporate-law director-residency rules and beneficial-owner disclosure requirements may apply depending on the incorporating statute and corporate profile.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada has no statutory requirement to surrender export proceeds to a Canadian bank, no mandatory conversion ratio, and no general statutory deadline for converting foreign-currency export receipts. Export proceeds may generally be retained in foreign-currency accounts or converted at the company's discretion, subject to contractual settlement terms, accounting requirements, tax reporting, sanctions controls, and bank monitoring. Canadian banks may request invoices, contracts, payment explanations, shipping or service-delivery evidence, and beneficial-owner information for unusual or high-value receipts. Cash or monetary-instrument movements of CAD 10,000 or more across the Canadian border are subject to reporting by the relevant carrier or traveller under applicable customs and proceeds-of-crime rules; this threshold does not create an export-receipt conversion obligation.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium for supplementary collection, payout, and foreign-currency functionality; low as the sole Canadian treasury bank. An offshore electronic-money institution cannot automatically provide Canadian deposit-taking, payment, foreign-exchange, or money-services functionality to Canadian residents without the required Canadian regulatory basis, registrations, exemptions, safeguarding arrangements, and consumer or payment-law compliance. A foreign platform may be usable for corporate treasury only after confirming its licensing jurisdiction, permitted cross-border services, Canadian solicitation status, funds safeguarding, sanctions controls, data handling, and settlement access. It should not replace a Canadian bank account for Canadian payroll, tax remittances, Apple or Google settlement reconciliation, operating expenses, or regulated payment activity. Any Canadian money-services-business activity may trigger registration and compliance obligations under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act and related regulations.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical attendance by directors is not universally mandated for Canadian corporate account opening. Remote onboarding may be available for straightforward corporations with Canadian banking relationships, digitally verifiable directors, and transparent Canadian operations. Banks may require a branch meeting, video interview, notarized or certified identification, Canadian-resident signing authority, or enhanced review where the company is newly incorporated, foreign-owned, digitally operated, has non-resident directors, receives substantial cross-border funds, uses complex ownership, or presents a high-risk geography or payment profile. The bank determines the final process under its risk-based AML program.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unclear beneficial ownership, nominee shareholders, layered holding companies, or inconsistent ownership between corporate records and onboarding forms
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified articles and certificates of incorporation, current corporate registry profile, corporate structure chart to the ultimate natural persons, shareholder register, registers of individuals with significant control where applicable, shareholder agreements, identification and address evidence for each beneficial owner, director resolutions, and a signed beneficial-ownership certification.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident ownership or directors with no credible Canadian operating nexus
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Business plan, Quebec and federal registration evidence, registered office and operating address, explanation of Canadian management and personnel, contracts with Canadian vendors or customers, tax-account registrations, expected Canadian transaction flows, director biographies, source-of-funds evidence, and a written rationale for the selected Canadian entity and bank.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Voice-streaming and social-app model perceived as high-risk user-generated-content, adult-content, gambling, virtual-asset, or anonymous-payment activity
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Detailed product description, terms of service, prohibited-content policy, age-assurance controls, moderation and escalation procedures, trust-and-safety governance, app-store approvals, payment-processor contracts, chargeback controls, refund policy, privacy compliance materials, evidence that the company does not operate gambling, virtual-currency exchange, money transmission, or adult-content services unless separately authorized.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Large or unexplained inbound receipts from Apple, Google, advertisers, foreign shareholders, or payment processors
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Platform agreements, payout statements, invoices, settlement reports, transaction-level reconciliations, merchant-of-record analysis, tax forms, shareholder subscription agreements, loan agreements, board approvals, source-of-funds evidence, expected monthly volumes, currencies, countries, and purpose narrative.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Sanctions, politically exposed person, adverse-media, fraud, or high-risk-country exposure
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Complete identity and ownership records, sanctions-screening results, PEP declarations, country-risk matrix, customer and vendor screening policy, payment approval matrix, transaction-monitoring procedures, escalation records, and documented exclusion of prohibited counterparties and jurisdictions.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Mismatch between declared business activity and actual payment flows or use of personal accounts
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Board-approved treasury policy, bank-account mandate, segregation of corporate and personal funds, accounting ledger, monthly bank reconciliations, revenue-flow map, payment-processor statements, source-and-use-of-funds schedule, and corrective-action evidence for any historical commingling.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Insufficient source of wealth or source of funds for paid-in capital, shareholder loans, or recurring shareholder support
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Audited or management financial statements, investor subscription documents, bank statements, financing agreements, tax returns where appropriate, sale or dividend evidence, investment-fund records, board resolutions, and a funds-flow diagram showing origin, intermediate accounts, and final Canadian account.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Expected transaction volumes materially exceed the forecast submitted during onboarding
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Updated rolling cash-flow forecast, revised platform settlement projections, customer and vendor concentration analysis, management accounts, explanation of volume variance, board approval, updated AML risk assessment, and advance notice to the bank's relationship and compliance teams.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Route equity through a regulated Canadian bank by SWIFT or correspondent-bank wire to the corporation's Canadian account. Use a clear payment reference such as 'equity subscription', 'capital contribution', or 'shareholder loan', consistent with the legal documents; Canada does not generally use a mandatory nationwide FX purpose-code system for ordinary commercial wires. Before receipt, provide the bank with the subscription agreement or loan agreement, board or shareholder approval, beneficial-owner information, source-of-funds evidence, remitter details, expected amount and currency, and the intended use of funds. The corporation should record the receipt consistently in its minute book and accounting records, issue shares or recognize debt as legally documented, reconcile the bank credit to the remittance advice, and assess thin-capitalization, transfer-pricing, withholding-tax, interest deductibility, and related-party reporting consequences. Do not route capital through personal accounts, unrelated third parties, anonymous wallets, or unexplained payment intermediaries. Incoming wires may be screened, held, returned, or reported where AML, sanctions, fraud, or correspondent-bank concerns arise.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Use Canadian-bank domestic EFT, wire transfer, or SWIFT MT103 for ordinary foreign supplier, contractor, cloud-hosting, advertising, platform, and professional-service payments. Each payment file should include the legal payee name, verified bank details, invoice or contract number, service description, currency, tax treatment, and sanctions screening result. Use commercial letters of credit, standby letters of credit, or documentary collections only where supplier risk, jurisdictional risk, or contractual requirements justify the cost; a commercial LC should specify issuing and confirming banks, documentary conditions, shipment or service evidence, expiry, discrepancy rules, governing law, and sanctions clauses. For a software and voice-streaming application, ordinary service wires and card or platform settlement arrangements will normally be more appropriate than documentary trade instruments. Maintain segregation of duties, dual approval, callback verification for bank-detail changes, vendor-master controls, monthly reconciliations, and documentation supporting cross-border withholding-tax and transfer-pricing positions.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Deliverable foreign-exchange forwards with a Canadian bank or other appropriately regulated counterparty, used to hedge documented forecast or committed exposures and supported by a treasury policy, exposure register, maturity limits, counterparty limits, and confirmation controls.

Non-deliverable forwards for currencies or jurisdictions where deliverable settlement is restricted or impractical, subject to counterparty eligibility, applicable Canadian securities and derivatives rules, Quebec requirements administered by the Autorité des marchés financiers where relevant, and documented commercial hedging purpose. NDF availability is currency- and counterparty-dependent.

Foreign-exchange swaps for short-term liquidity management or rolling currency funding, subject to counterparty documentation, valuation, collateral or margin terms, accounting treatment, and applicable derivatives requirements.

Currency options and collars may be available for documented commercial exposures, but they require enhanced suitability, valuation, premium, accounting, and risk-governance controls and should not be used for speculative trading.

Cross-currency swaps may be used for longer-term funding or recurring currency exposure where the notional, maturity, collateral, termination, benchmark, and accounting risks are approved by the board or treasury committee.

Hedging should be limited to identifiable operating, capital, financing, or committed revenue exposures; speculative derivatives activity, unapproved leverage, personal dealing, and transactions with unregulated or opaque counterparties should be prohibited.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Declaration (Déclaration annuelle) under the Quebec Business Corporations Act (QBCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the end of the corporation's fiscal year; for a calendar-year corporation, by March 1 of the following year (fiscal year end December 31)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty and formal default notation under the LPLE fee schedule; the REQ issues a delinquency notice and, if the declaration remains outstanding, may administratively dissolve the corporation. No attestation de conformité (certificate of compliance) can be issued while the corporation is in default.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Federal Annual Return under the Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporations Canada (Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days after the anniversary date of incorporation each calendar year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to file for two consecutive years authorizes administrative dissolution under s.226 CBCA; revival under s.225 CBCA is available within 10 years, but the corporation loses legal capacity and directors may incur liability for debts contracted during the dissolution period.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual confirmation of the Register of Individuals with Significant Control (UBO register) and share-transfer updates
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Registraire des entreprises du Québec (REQ) and Corporations Canada; register maintained at the registered office for inspection
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: UBO register entries must be updated within 15 days of a share transfer or control change; annual confirmation is embedded in the Quebec annual declaration and federal annual return deadlines above
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Contraventions are offences under s.152.4 CBCA (summary fine up to CAD 200,000 and/or six months imprisonment) and under the QBCA transparency regime; persistent non-compliance invalidates registry compliance attestations and corporate good-standing status.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No revenue or asset threshold triggers the audit: CBCA and QBCA corporations must appoint an independent auditor at each annual meeting unless all shareholders, including non-voting shareholders, pass a unanimous resolution waiving the audit for that fiscal year. Reporting issuers and distributing corporations cannot waive. A private voice-streaming app corporation may therefore avoid a statutory audit on unanimous annual shareholder consent.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Reporting issuers must use IFRS as adopted in Canada; eligible private corporations may elect either Canadian ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises) or IFRS for their general-purpose financial statements.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Under the QBCA and CBCA, the register of individuals with significant control (holders of 25% or more, or persons with de facto significant control) must be updated within 15 days of any share transfer or change in control. Each annual declaration and annual return requires a certification that the UBO register is complete and accurate; share transfers occurring during the fiscal year must be journalized in the transfer register before the annual confirmation is signed.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Members, Register of Directors, Minute Book
Register of Individuals with Significant Control (UBO Register)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 120–400 per year (CAD 150–500 typical) for a Quebec registered office or corporate agent service
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 5,000–15,000 per year for an independent audit by a licensed Quebec CPA firm; USD 2,000–4,000 per year for a review engagement where the unanimous shareholder waiver is used

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 26.5% combined general corporate rate: 15% federal (Income Tax Act, Part I, s. 123) plus 11.5% Quebec provincial (Taxation Act, s. 771). A Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) benefits from a combined 12.2% rate on the first C$500,000 of active business income (9% federal small business deduction + 3.2% Quebec small business deduction), but this is unavailable where the corporation is controlled, in law or in fact, by non-residents (e.g., a US parent).
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: No statutory tax holiday exists for software or digital audio platforms in Canada or Quebec. Available preferential instruments: (i) Federal SR&ED investment tax credit: 35% refundable for eligible CCPCs (15% non-refundable for non-CCPCs) on qualifying R&D labour and direct expenditures; (ii) Quebec SR&ED tax credit: 14% general refundable credit, up to 30% refundable for small and medium-sized enterprises on the first C$3,000,000 of qualifying expenditures; (iii) Quebec Interactive Digital Media (IDM) tax credit: up to 27.5% of eligible multimedia labour and qualifying software expenditures (30% to 32.5% in designated metropolitan and resource regions), potentially applicable to an interactive voice-streaming social application; (iv) the federal general rate of 15% already reflects the federal-provincial abatement; (v) for a foreign-controlled subsidiary, the small business deduction and the enhanced 35% refundable SR&ED rate are not available.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (federal) with CRA Schedules 1, 5, 8, 91 and supporting Forms T106, T1134 and NR4; filed electronically through CRA My Business Account or a CRA-certified T2 E-file / XML filing service.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual (fiscal period; a fiscal period may not exceed 53 weeks). Interim federal tax instalments are due monthly for non-CCPCs and quarterly for qualifying CCPCs, computed under the prior-year, current-year or no-due-date instalment baseline.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: T2 must be filed no later than six months after the end of the taxation year (e.g., December 31 year-end is due by June 30). The balance of federal corporate tax is due two months after year-end for a non-CCPC and three months after year-end for an eligible CCPC; Quebec balance payment follows the parallel calendar.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Legal name, Business Number (BN) with RC program identifier, Quebec NEQ (14 digits), fiscal year start and end, corporate status, registered office address and principal business activity code (NAICS 519130 / ISIC 6311).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Indicate that the corporation is a Canadian subsidiary of a non-resident parent; answer 'no' to the Canadian-controlled private corporation question; complete shareholder disclosure showing the ultimate foreign parent and percentage of voting control.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross revenue from voice-streaming subscriptions, in-app purchases, Apple IAP and Google Play Billing proceeds, virtual gifting, advertising and royalties, reported on an accrual basis in Canadian dollars.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Do not net the 15% or 30% app-store commission against revenue; report the store commission separately as a deductible selling expense. Where IP royalties are payable to the foreign parent, isolate licensed royalty income on separate disclosure schedules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: All deductible operating expenses: app-store commissions, content acquisition, bandwidth and streaming hosting, payroll, marketing, professional fees, depreciation/amortization, interest and management fees.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Deduct app-store commissions only where invoiced to the Canadian entity; flag all related-party royalty, management, technology-service and interest payments so that Schedule 1 Part VIII and Form T106 disclosure are completed contemporaneously.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Reconciliation of accounting net income to taxable income under Schedule 1; includes 50% of capital gains, deductions for non-capital loss carryforwards, SR&ED expenditure adjustments and transfer pricing corrections.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Claim non-capital loss carryforwards of prior Canadian taxation years (20-year federal carryforward / 3-year carryback); adjust for Part XIII withholdings attributable to payments to non-residents; do not claim the CCPC small business deduction in a foreign-controlled entity.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 1 - Part A, Lines 55-80: Federal tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Federal corporate income tax calculated at the 15% general rate (9% for qualifying CCPC active business income up to C$500,000) plus Part IV tax on portfolio dividends, with provincial allocation in Schedule 5.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a US-parent-controlled non-CCPC, apply the full 15% general rate; attach Schedule 91 (information on parent/corporate ownership) and Form T1134, and document the arm's-length basis of every intercompany transaction to support the s. 247(3) 'reasonable efforts' defence.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing: 5% of unpaid federal tax plus 1% per full month up to 12 months (s. 162(1) ITA); gross negligence penalty: 50% of tax avoided or misclaimed (s. 163(2)); daily compound interest at the CRA prescribed rate on unpaid balances (s. 161). Late or deficient T106 filing attracts C$25-per-day penalties up to C$2,500 and additional fixed penalties.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Form CO-17 Corporate Income Tax Return (Revenu Quebec) with accompanying schedules CO-17.S, CO-1166 and CO-1029; filed electronically through Revenu Quebec's 'La societe en ligne' portal using the Quebec Enterprise Number (NEQ).
tax_return_filing_anatomy.reporting_frequency: Annual, aligned with the federal T2 fiscal period. Quebec instalments are required under the Taxation Act where provincial tax exceeds the statutory threshold, due on the first day of each quarter.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: CO-17 must be filed within six months of the end of the fiscal year. The balance of Quebec corporate income tax is due within two months of the fiscal year-end for a non-CCPC and three months for an eligible CCPC; instalment schedules mirror the federal pattern.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: NEQ (Quebec enterprise number), legal name, fiscal period, principal business activity, registered office, and ultimate parent information.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Identify the ultimate parent as the foreign (e.g., US) corporation; indicate the date of Quebec registration and whether the corporation is exempt from the Quebec small business deduction because it is controlled by non-residents.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Quebec-computed business income and deductions, including app-store commissions, streaming costs, payroll, financing charges and intercompany payments, reconciled to the T2 amounts.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Mirror the federal taxable income before Quebec adjustments; show in the reconciliation any Part XIII tax withheld by the corporation on dividends and royalties paid to the foreign parent; ensure the Quebec share of provincial allocation is correctly computed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Deduction for non-capital loss carryforwards and adjusted tax losses available under the Taxation Act.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Use only Quebec-qualified losses; do not infer deductibility from a federal loss balance where provincial rules differ for foreign-controlled corporations.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Provincial corporate income tax computed at the 11.5% general rate (3.2% for eligible small-business income of a CCPC); tax credits such as the Quebec SR&ED credit and IDM multimedia credit are applied at this line.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-CCPC subsidiary, apply 11.5%; if CRA reassesses transfer pricing, Revenu Quebec will ordinarily follow the federal adjustment under coordinated tax treaties and joint audit protocols.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Revenu Quebec late-filing penalty: 5% of unpaid provincial tax plus 1% per full month up to 12 months (Tax Administration Act, RLRQ c. L-1.1, s. 1031); daily compound interest at the Quebec prescribed rate; willful evasion penalties of 50% to 150% and imprisonment for tax offences.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 25% under Part XIII of the Income Tax Act (s. 212(2)) on dividends paid by a Canadian resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder. Quebec imposes no separate dividend withholding tax on non-residents, as the federal Part XIII tax is shared with the province. Under the Canada-US tax treaty (Article X): 5% for dividends paid to a US corporation that beneficially owns at least 10% of the voting shares; otherwise 15%.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke treaty-reduced withholding: (i) obtain from the non-resident payee, before or at the time of payment, a completed Form NR301 declaration of entitlement to benefits together with a current Certificate of Residence (TRC) issued by the US Internal Revenue Service or the relevant foreign tax authority; (ii) withhold at the reduced treaty rate only where the beneficial-ownership and limitation-on-benefits conditions are met; (iii) remit withheld amounts to the CRA by the 15th day of the month following the payment month using the NR4 remittance system; (iv) file Form NR4 and the NR4 Summary by March 31 of the following calendar year; (v) maintain ownership and residency evidence for six years to discharge CRA audit and treaty-shelter scrutiny.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory Part XIII rates: royalties 25% (s. 212(1)(d)) and interest 25% (s. 212(1)(b)). Canada-US treaty rates: copyright and qualifying software royalties 0% (Article XII(1)); patent, trademark, know-how and industrial royalties 10% (Article XII(2)); arm's-length interest 0% (Article XI), with related-party contingent interest subject to 15% where specific treaty conditions are not satisfied; for non-treaty jurisdictions, the full 25% statutory rates apply.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Form T106 Information Return is mandatory where the aggregate fair market value of reportable non-arm's-length cross-border transactions with non-residents exceeds C$1,000,000 in a taxation year. Contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation (the CRA 'Local File' standard per Information Circular IC 87-2R) should be prepared for all material intercompany transactions to sustain the 'reasonable efforts' defence against the s. 247(3) penalty. A mandatory Master File applies to fiscal years beginning after 2021 for multinational enterprise groups with consolidated group revenue of at least C$1,000,000,000. Country-by-Country Reporting obligations arise for fiscal years beginning after 2015 where the MNE group's consolidated revenue is at least C$750,000,000.
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not apply standalone Economic Substance Regulations (ESR regimes are specific to offshore financial centres such as the UAE and BVI). The functional Canadian equivalents are: (i) the statutory General Anti-Avoidance Rule (s. 245 ITA) invalidating abusive avoidance transactions lacking genuine economic substance; (ii) judicial substance-over-form and 'sham' transaction doctrines; (iii) the corporate-residence test based on central management and control; (iv) anti-treaty-shopping jurisprudence and OECD BEPS minimum standards applied by CRA; (v) permanent establishment risk: a Quebec voice-streaming operation with local staff, servers or editorial control may create a Canadian PE for the foreign parent, exposing profits to Part I/Part XIV tax. A Quebec corporation holding nominal staffing, no board activity and all IP offshore will attract GAAR re-characterization of intercompany royalties and management fees.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberate understatement of Apple IAP and Google Play Billing revenues (including netting app-store commissions, mischaracterizing in-app voice gifts as non-taxable gratuities, unreported virtual-currency settlement), fabrication of expenses, and misdeclaration of the foreign parent's Canadian permanent establishment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Income Tax Act s. 239(1): fine of between 50% and 200% of the evaded tax plus imprisonment for up to five years; s. 163(2) gross negligence penalty of 50% of tax avoided or misclaimed; GAAR reversal under s. 245 and reassessment within the normal or extended statutory periods; Quebec Tax Administration Act penalties of 50% to 150% and imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and senior officers who signed or directed false filings are jointly and severally liable for the corporation's tax arrears, penalties and interest; courts pierce the corporate veil on fraud; criminal conviction may trigger travel bans pending sentencing, asset seizure and forced sale of personal property, and extradition exposure where offshore proceeds are concealed.
